paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The measurement problem is the puzzle of definite outcomes in quantum mechanics. A quantum system can be in a superposition, a blend of different states, and its wave function changes over time in a fully predictable way set by the Schrödinger equation. Yet every real measurement finds the system in one definite state. The problem is to explain how a superposition of many possible values turns into one measured value.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is a puzzle
paragraphs.text: After a measurement, the wave function carries on from whatever state the system was found in. So the act of measuring seems to have done something to the system that does not plainly follow from the Schrödinger equation. Put another way, that equation fixes the wave function at every later time. If observers and their instruments are also described by such a predictable wave function, why can we predict only probabilities rather than exact results?

paragraphs.heading: The cat in the box
paragraphs.text: The thought experiment called Schrödinger's cat shows the problem. A device is rigged to kill a cat if a quantum event happens, such as a radioactive atom decaying, and both are shut in a chamber. Until someone looks, quantum mechanics treats the atom as a superposition of decayed and intact, so the cat too becomes a mix of an intact atom with a live cat and a decayed atom with a dead one. But open the chamber and the cat is simply alive or dead, with no superposition in sight. That raises more questions: when does a measurement happen, what counts as a measuring device, and what part does the observer play?

paragraphs.heading: The Copenhagen answer
paragraphs.text: The oldest response, and probably still the most widely held, is the group of views called the Copenhagen interpretation. These views hold that something in the act of observing makes the wave function collapse. The idea is often credited to Niels Bohr but in fact came from Werner Heisenberg. In this tradition a wave function can be treated as statistical information about a system, and collapse is the updating of that information when new data comes in. Exactly how to understand this is still argued over.

paragraphs.heading: Many worlds
paragraphs.text: Hugh Everett's many-worlds interpretation tries to make the problem disappear. In its view the whole universe is described by a single wave function, one vast superposition that never collapses. A measurement is then only an interaction in which quantum things, such as an observer, an instrument and an electron, become entangled into one bigger whole. Its supporters have still not agreed on how to justify using the Born rule to get probabilities.

paragraphs.heading: Hidden paths and real collapse
paragraphs.text: The de Broglie–Bohm theory takes another route: besides the wave function, a system carries extra data, a trajectory giving where its particles are. The wave function's job is to set the particles' velocities. During a measurement, contact with the surroundings separates the wave packets, which looks like collapse even though none truly happens. Objective-collapse models instead change the Schrödinger equation itself by adding random nonlinear terms. For electrons or atoms these make no measurable difference, but for large objects they become important and cause collapse.
